explanation: Because children have lower physical reserves, a minor illness or breathing problem can quickly turn serious if we don't catch it early. You're building great clinical intuition! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of an obstetric emergency?

options.A: Severe postpartum hemorrhage
options.B: Chronic knee osteoarthritis
options.C: A mild seasonal allergy
options.D: Routine pregnancy checkup

explanation: Heavy bleeding after childbirth is a life-threatening emergency unique to obstetric care. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary goal of nursing care during a psychiatric or behavioral emergency?

options.A: Proving the patient is at fault for their behavior
options.B: Immediately discharging the patient to home
options.C: Starting long-term psychotherapy in the emergency bay
options.D: Ensuring safety and de-escalating the crisis

explanation: Keeping everyone safe and calming the patient down is always your first priority in any mental health emergency. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h5)

question: When should physical or chemical restraints be used during a behavioral crisis?

options.A: Whenever the nursing staff feels mildly inconvenienced
options.B: As the very first step for any agitated patient
options.C: As a last resort when safety is at immediate risk
options.D: Only when ordered by a family member

explanation: Restraints are restrictive and carry risks, so they are only used when all verbal de-escalation fails and someone is in danger of being hurt. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h5)

question: What defines a mass casualty incident (MCI)?

options.A: An emergency that only happens inside a surgical theatre
options.B: A routine medical ward shift with high patient turnover
options.C: Any situation where a single patient arrives in an ambulance
options.D: Patient numbers and injuries overwhelm available local resources

explanation: An MCI happens when the scale of the emergency outstrips the normal staff, space, and supplies of the hospital or clinic. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h6)

question: How does triage during a mass casualty incident differ from everyday emergency department triage?

options.A: It completely ignores patients with bleeding wounds
options.B: It takes much longer per patient because detailed medical histories are collected
options.C: It is performed exclusively by hospital administrators sitting in offices
options.D: It focuses on saving the greatest number with limited resources rather than treating everyone with maximum effort

explanation: In a mass casualty incident, the goal shifts to saving as many lives as possible using fast sorting methods, rather than spending all resources on one critical patient. Brilliant effort! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of emergency nursing when managing a life-threatening condition?

options.A: Conducting routine diagnostic laboratory tests
options.B: Completing a full health history before acting
options.C: Discharging the patient as quickly as possible
options.D: Rapid identification and immediate intervention

explanation: Emergency nursing focuses on acting fast to save lives when a patient's condition can quickly deteriorate. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is time considered so critical when dealing with emergency medical conditions?

options.A: Hospital regulations require fast bed turnover
options.B: Insurance companies will not pay for slow care
options.C: Doctors refuse to see patients who wait too long
options.D: Delays can lead to rapid deterioration and death

explanation: In critical emergencies, minutes matter because a failing body system quickly causes permanent harm or death if not supported. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h1)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the ABCDE emergency assessment framework?

options.A: Brain function
options.B: Blood pressure
options.C: Bleeding
options.D: Breathing

explanation: The ABCDE acronym stands for Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, and Exposure. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient arrives in the emergency unit after a severe motorcycle crash. According to the ABCDE rule, what should the nurse check first?

options.A: Blood pressure
options.B: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.C: Airway patency
options.D: Hidden skin wounds

explanation: Airway is always the top priority in the ABCDE approach because an obstructed airway causes death faster than anything else. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which sign is a clinical indicator of severe respiratory distress in an adult patient?

options.A: Relaxed posture in a flat bed
options.B: Slow and deep regular breathing
options.C: Use of accessory neck muscles
options.D: Warm and pink skin coloration

explanation: When breathing becomes very hard, patients use their neck and chest muscles to help force air in and out. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why is a silent chest in a patient with severe asthma considered a dangerous emergency?

options.A: It means air is no longer moving in or out of the lungs
options.B: It is a normal finding during deep sleep
options.C: It shows that the inhaler medication worked successfully
options.D: It indicates the asthma attack has completely resolved

explanation: A silent chest means the airways are so tight or blocked that air cannot move at all, which signals immediate respiratory arrest. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is a primary clinical feature of hemodynamic instability?

options.A: High fever with shivering and chills
options.B: Elevated urine output above normal limits
options.C: Gradual weight gain over several weeks
options.D: Inadequate blood flow to vital organs

explanation: Hemodynamic instability simply means the circulation is failing to supply enough blood to keep organs working properly. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why can a normal blood pressure reading sometimes be misleading in early cardiovascular shock?

options.A: Only the pulse rate matters during a cardiac crisis
options.B: Heart conditions never affect blood pressure numbers
options.C: The body's compensation keeps pressure normal before it crashes
options.D: Blood pressure cuffs are notoriously inaccurate in emergency rooms

explanation: The body works hard to keep blood pressure stable by narrowing blood vessels, meaning the patient can suddenly crash later. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h4)

question: What is the underlying physiological problem in all types of shock?

options.A: Chronic inflammation of the joints
options.B: Inadequate tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia
options.C: An excess of oxygen in the circulating blood
options.D: A sudden increase in overall body temperature

explanation: Shock occurs when cells do not receive enough oxygen-rich blood to perform normal metabolism. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h5)

question: A patient with severe internal bleeding from a car crash is most likely to develop which type of shock?

options.A: Neurogenic shock
options.B: Hypovolemic shock
options.C: Anaphylactic shock
options.D: Cardiogenic shock

explanation: Hypovolemic shock is caused by a drastic loss of blood volume circulating in the body. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which quick bedside test should a nurse perform immediately for any patient presenting with sudden confusion?

options.A: Blood glucose test
options.B: Chest X-ray imaging
options.C: Electrocardiogram test
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: Low blood sugar is a common, easily reversible cause of altered mental status that must be checked right away. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h6)

question: What do the letters in the FAST stroke mnemonic stand for to help recognize warning signs?

options.A: Fluid intake, Activity level, Skin turgor, Eyes check
options.B: Fast breathing, Airway blockage, Sound tone, Temperature
options.C: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call
options.D: Fever, Aches, Stiffness, Tiredness

explanation: FAST is a simple public health tool used to spot the most common stroke symptoms quickly. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h6)

question: Which major organ system is most immediately threatened by severe hyperkalemia (high blood potassium)?

options.A: Skeletal muscle system
options.B: Gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Cardiovascular system
options.D: Integumentary system

explanation: High potassium levels dangerously alter the electrical conduction of the heart, leading to fatal arrhythmias. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following conditions is a classic example of a metabolic crisis in diabetes?

options.A: Prolonged hypoglycemia
options.B: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.C: Diabetic neuropathy
options.D: Chronic foot ulceration

explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis is an acute, life-threatening metabolic emergency caused by severe insulin deficiency and acid buildup. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h7)

question: Why is continuous re-evaluation necessary in emergency nursing care?

options.A: Patient conditions can change rapidly and unpredictably
options.B: Hospital policies require charting every fifteen minutes
options.C: Patients get bored if nurses do not check on them
options.D: Doctors will not review charts without new updates

explanation: Emergency patients are unstable, meaning a stable patient can deteriorate suddenly and require a shift in priorities. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h8)

question: A nurse is caring for four emergency patients. Which patient should the nurse attend to FIRST?

options.A: A patient with a minor scalp laceration needing stitches
options.B: A patient with a closed wrist fracture in mild pain
options.C: A patient with severe stridor and throat swelling
options.D: A patient complaining of a mild headache for three days

explanation: Stridor indicates an upper airway obstruction, which is an immediate life threat that takes top priority over pain or minor injuries. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h8)

question: What is the main thing that sets a medical emergency apart from a trauma case?

options.A: It is always caused by a blunt or penetrating external force
options.B: It occurs exclusively in patients with a history of surgery
options.C: It develops slowly over several months without sudden changes
options.D: It arises from internal disease processes or system breakdown

explanation: Think of medical emergencies as coming from within—like an organ failure or sudden illness—while trauma comes from outside forces. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which of these options is a classic example of a traumatic emergency?

options.A: A bone fracture and heavy bleeding following a motor crash
options.B: A sudden stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain
options.C: A severe asthma attack triggered by dust in the ward
options.D: A sudden drop in blood sugar leading to a diabetic coma

explanation: Trauma involves physical force from the outside world, such as a vehicle crash. Great job spotting the difference! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h1)

question: During a community disease outbreak, what is the main cause of biological hazard emergencies?

options.A: Accidental leakage of industrial gas from factories
options.B: Sudden heavy rainfall flooding residential areas
options.C: Rapid spread of infectious diseases among populations
options.D: Widespread consumption of expired tinned foods

explanation: Biological hazards are living microscopic troublemakers like bacteria and viruses that spread fast through communities. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h2)

question: A farmer arrives at the clinic with severe muscle twitching and too much saliva after working in the fields. What caused this?

options.A: A natural disaster caused by flooding
options.B: A chemical exposure from pesticides
options.C: A traumatic injury from a falling tree branch
options.D: A biological outbreak of meningitis

explanation: Pesticides are powerful chemicals that affect the nervous system, leading to symptoms like twitching and excess saliva. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the leading cause of severe trauma and head injuries on our roads here in Nigeria?

options.A: Road traffic accidents
options.B: Severe seasonal flooding
options.C: Industrial chemical spills
options.D: Household gas explosions

explanation: Sadly, road traffic accidents are the top reason emergency wards see severe injuries. Stay safe out there! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h3)

question: A child swallowed a brightly colored liquid from a soft drink bottle. What is the nurse's most important first step?

options.A: Place the child flat on their back to rest quietly
options.B: Induce vomiting immediately to remove the liquid
options.C: Identify the exact substance swallowed without delaying care
options.D: Administer large amounts of palm oil to neutralize the poison

explanation: Knowing the exact poison helps the doctor give the right treatment. Never force vomiting for chemicals, as it can cause worse burns on the way back up! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h3)

question: In simple terms, what does cellular hypoxia mean for the body's tissues?

options.A: An excess of sugar circulating in the blood
options.B: A dangerous shortage of oxygen supply
options.C: A sudden increase in total body water volume
options.D: A high concentration of red blood cells

explanation: Hypo means low, and oxia refers to oxygen. It simply means the cells are crying out for the oxygen they need to work! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why does losing a massive amount of blood lead straight into shock?

options.A: The kidneys stop producing urine to save salt and water
options.B: Red blood cells multiply too fast and block small blood vessels
options.C: The heart beats too slowly to pump blood to the lungs
options.D: There is not enough fluid volume to maintain perfusion pressure

explanation: Without enough fluid in the pipes, the blood pressure drops, and vital organs don't get the blood flow they need. You're mastering the core concepts! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which group of people is most at risk of sudden, severe dehydration from diarrhea?

options.A: Young healthy adult males
options.B: Children under five years old
options.C: Adolescents in secondary school
options.D: Elderly men with chronic cough

explanation: Little ones have small body reserves and lose water very quickly. That's why childhood diarrhea is treated as an urgent matter! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is a major non-medical challenge that delays emergency survival in many developing areas?

options.A: Strict government regulations on the use of intravenous fluids
options.B: A lack of interest in modern medicine among rural community members
options.C: Delays in reaching a health facility due to financial and transport challenges
options.D: Excessive availability of free ambulance services on major roads

explanation: Transportation bottlenecks and money hurdles often delay patients from getting to the hospital on time. Every minute counts in an emergency! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h5)

question: When doing a quick ABCDE emergency check on a patient, what does the letter 'C' stand for?

options.A: Coughing
options.B: Circulation
options.C: Consciousness
options.D: Cyanosis

explanation: A is Airway, B is Breathing, and C is Circulation! You check pulses and bleeding here. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h6)

question: An unconscious patient is brought to the ward. After checking their airway and breathing, which scale should you use to assess their brain function and alertness?

options.A: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.B: Sphygmomanometer
options.C: Body mass index chart
options.D: Peak flow meter

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is our trusty bedside tool for checking a patient's level of consciousness. You'll use this a lot in clinicals! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why do nurses prefer using large-bore IV catheters when handling emergency resuscitation?

options.A: They allow rapid infusion of fluids and emergency drugs
options.B: They can remain inside the vein for up to two weeks safely
options.C: They prevent the need to monitor blood pressure regularly
options.D: They cause less pain when inserted into small arm veins

explanation: A wider tube means fluids can rush in much faster to save a crashing patient. Smart thinking! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the best immediate nursing action for an unconscious patient who is breathing on their own?

options.A: Force fluids by mouth to prevent dehydration during sleep
options.B: Place them in the recovery position to keep the airway clear
options.C: Prop them upright in bed to encourage deep lung breathing
options.D: Tie their arms to the bed rails to prevent sudden movement

explanation: The recovery position keeps the tongue from blocking the airway and lets saliva drain out safely. A classic life-saving nursing skill! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the main sign that a medical situation is a true life-threatening emergency?

options.A: Any illness that requires admission to a private room
options.B: Any injury that causes moderate joint and muscle pain
options.C: Immediate failure of one or more vital organ systems
options.D: A chronic condition that lasts longer than six months

explanation: Life-threatening emergencies mean vital organs are shutting down fast. Without quick help, this can lead to serious danger. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why do nurses look beyond the obvious symptoms when a patient's condition is crashing?

options.A: To ensure the hospital billing department receives correct insurance data
options.B: Because lab technicians require secondary confirmation for all tests
options.C: So that family members can be discharged home earlier in the shift
options.D: Because primary organ failure quickly triggers a cascade affecting other systems

explanation: When one major organ starts failing, it quickly pulls other vital systems down with it. Checking the whole patient keeps you steps ahead! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h1)

question: What makes blunt force trauma to the abdomen so dangerous?

options.A: Permanent stiffening of the peripheral joints
options.B: Immediate infection of the superficial skin layers
options.C: Rapid development of severe seasonal allergies
options.D: Massive internal bleeding without visible external wounds

explanation: A person can look fine on the outside while bleeding heavily inside. That's why careful, hands-on nursing assessment is always key! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h2)

question: How does a tension pneumothorax cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure?

options.A: Trapped chest air compresses the heart and large blood vessels, reducing blood return
options.B: The patient stops breathing entirely due to complete paralysis of the diaphragm
options.C: Air travels directly into the bloodstream and dissolves all red blood cells
options.D: Fluid fills the lung tissue and drowns the patient from the inside out

explanation: Think of trapped air in the chest like a tight clamp pressing down on the heart and major blood vessels, stopping blood from flowing properly. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the main problem when the heart suddenly fails to pump properly?

options.A: An immediate and permanent increase in body temperature
options.B: Complete paralysis of the skeletal muscles in the lower limbs
options.C: Uncontrolled overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.D: A dangerous drop in systemic blood pressure and oxygen delivery

explanation: If the heart pump slows or stops, pressure drops and oxygen stops reaching the tissues that need it most. Spotting this early saves lives! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h3)

question: A patient arrives with a massive pulmonary embolism. What is happening in their body?

options.A: Blood flow through the pulmonary arteries is blocked, impairing oxygenation
options.B: The liver has stopped producing clotting factors, causing widespread bleeding
options.C: An infection in the urinary tract has spread into the spinal fluid
options.D: Gastric acid is leaking directly into the peritoneal cavity through an ulcer

explanation: A pulmonary embolism is a blocked blood vessel in the lungs. Because the blockage is there, blood can't pick up fresh oxygen to circulate. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which part of the body suffers damage first when a person's airway is completely blocked?

options.A: Brain
options.B: Liver
options.C: Kidneys
options.D: Spleen

explanation: The brain uses up oxygen extremely fast! That is why the airway is always our number one priority in any emergency. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why does a severe opioid overdose lead to dangerous breathing problems?

options.A: It causes immediate physical swelling and closure of the main vocal cords
options.B: It depresses the respiratory control center in the brainstem, reducing breathing rate
options.C: It freezes the movement of the diaphragm muscle by destroying motor nerves
options.D: It triggers severe allergic bronchospasm in the small bronchial airways

explanation: Opioids affect the part of the brain that tells the body to breathe, causing breathing to slow down and eventually stop if untreated. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is a major effect of severe heatstroke on the body's cells?

options.A: Disruption of vital enzymatic reactions and cellular function
options.B: Complete cessation of electrical activity in the skeletal muscles
options.C: Rapid production of large quantities of protective body fat
options.D: Permanent freezing of blood vessels in the upper extremities

explanation: Extreme heat scrambles the delicate proteins and enzymes our cells need to work. Cooling the patient down quickly is a true medical emergency priority! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a normal way that toxic substances cause a medical emergency?

options.A: Disrupting cellular oxygen use at the tissue level
options.B: Blocking the normal electrical signals of the heart
options.C: Stimulating the production of healthy bone marrow cells
options.D: Causing sudden and profound systemic vasodilation

explanation: Making healthy blood cells in the bone marrow is a good, normal process! Toxins cause harm by damaging systems, not by boosting healthy growth. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h5)

question: When doing an emergency primary survey (ABCDE), what do you check first?

options.A: Circulation
options.B: Disability
options.C: Exposure
options.D: Airway

explanation: Always start with 'A' for Airway! Making sure air can move freely into the lungs comes before anything else. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h6)

question: An unresponsive patient is brought in. After you make sure their airway and breathing are okay, what is your next immediate step?

options.A: Inquiring about dietary preferences for hospital meals
options.B: Checking circulation, pulse rate, and blood pressure
options.C: Reviewing the patient's employment history and workplace
options.D: Measuring the exact height and weight on a scale

explanation: Following the ABCDE routine, 'C' comes right after Airway and Breathing so you can check for blood flow and signs of shock. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T4#GNS315_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the main goal of triage in a busy healthcare setting?

options.A: To sort patients and prioritize care based on urgency
options.B: To provide a complete medical diagnosis for every visitor
options.C: To collect insurance and billing information before treatment
options.D: To discharge minor cases without letting them see a doctor

explanation: Triage acts as your first safety filter when the ward is busy, ensuring the sickest patients get seen without dangerous delays. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to triage patients when the emergency department is packed?

options.A: Because hospital rules forbid seeing patients in the order they arrive
options.B: Because nurses need extra time to complete paperwork for each case
options.C: Because patient needs are greater than available staff and resources
options.D: Because doctors prefer to treat minor injuries before major trauma

explanation: When too many people arrive at once, triage helps match our limited hospital resources to the patients who need help the absolute most. Great thinking! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the golden rule of triage when responding to a major disaster?

options.A: Treating every single injured person in the exact order of arrival
options.B: Doing the greatest good for the greatest number of people
options.C: Sending all critical patients to the nearest small clinic
options.D: Focusing entirely on saving the person with the highest social status

explanation: In a disaster with scarce supplies, we shift our mindset from individual care to saving as many lives as our resources can possibly reach. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h2)

question: Why must a triage nurse keep checking on patients who are sitting in the waiting area?

options.A: Doctors refuse to start treatment without fresh paperwork
options.B: A stable patient's condition can worsen while they wait
options.C: Patients get angry if their vital signs are not checked twice an hour
options.D: Hospital management requires nurses to update charts every five minutes

explanation: Illness can change fast! Someone who looked fine a few minutes ago can suddenly take a turn for the worse. Regular checks keep everyone safe. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which triage category is meant for a patient who needs life-saving help right this second?

options.A: Resuscitation
options.B: Urgent
options.C: Non-urgent
options.D: Routine

explanation: Resuscitation is our highest alert level. Every single second counts here to keep the patient alive and stable! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h3)

question: A patient walks into the clinic with a mild ankle sprain and stable vital signs. What triage level fits best?

options.A: Urgent
options.B: Non-urgent
options.C: Resuscitation
options.D: Emergent

explanation: A stable injury that just needs a quick check or an X-ray falls right into our non-urgent category. Simple and straightforward! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h3)

question: How is disaster triage different from regular emergency department triage?

options.A: Routine triage is only used when there are zero available beds
options.B: Disaster triage focuses on saving the greatest number with limited resources
options.C: Routine triage ignores vital signs while disaster triage requires full lab work
options.D: Disaster triage gives highest priority to patients with the worst chance of survival

explanation: When mass casualties hit, our main goal shifts from giving maximum individual care to saving the maximum number of community lives. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h4)

question: During a building collapse with dozens of victims, a patient with severe, fatal injuries gets an expectant (black) tag. Why do we do this?

options.A: Because nurses are not legally allowed to touch trauma patients outdoors
options.B: To preserve scarce medical supplies for victims who have a better chance of survival
options.C: Because minor injuries always take legal precedence over head trauma
options.D: To punish the patient for not wearing safety equipment

explanation: This is one of the hardest parts of nursing, but when supplies are limited, we must focus our efforts where we can genuinely save lives. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is a common misunderstanding about the role of the triage nurse?

options.A: That triage nurses are responsible for performing major surgical procedures
options.B: That the triage nurse works exclusively in the hospital pharmacy
options.C: That it is merely a clerical desk job rather than a high-level clinical assessment
options.D: That triage staff never interact directly with incoming patients

explanation: Triage is real clinical nursing! It takes sharp assessment skills and quick thinking to spot hidden dangers at the front desk. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why is the triage nurse's job considered to carry big legal responsibilities?

options.A: A missed critical symptom during the initial sort can cause severe patient harm
options.B: Hospital insurance does not cover mistakes made outside the ward
options.C: Triage nurses must personally pay for any medication ordered at the desk
options.D: The nurse is legally required to diagnose every disease on arrival

explanation: Because triage is the very first stop, catching critical symptoms early protects the patient and keeps your clinical practice safe. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h5)

question: What quick assessment guide helps nurses check a new patient rapidly?

options.A: Detailed psychological background check
options.B: Nutritional and dietary history review
options.C: Comprehensive head-to-toe physical examination
options.D: Primary survey (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure)

explanation: ABCDE is your best friend in emergency nursing. It lets you spot and tackle life-threatening issues instantly! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h6)

question: How is a triage check different from a full ward admission assessment?

options.A: Triage assessment is rapid and focused on immediate life threats rather than being comprehensive
options.B: Admission assessments take less than two minutes to complete
options.C: Admission assessments are always performed by security guards instead of nurses
options.D: Triage assessment skips vital signs entirely and relies on guesswork

explanation: At triage, we don't have time for a lengthy life story. We scan for immediate dangers first, then dive deeper later! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which ethical principle guides triage nurses to treat every patient fairly, no matter their background?

options.A: Autonomy
options.B: Paternalism
options.C: Justice
options.D: Beneficence

explanation: Justice means treating everyone fairly and sharing our healthcare resources impartially, without any bias or favoritism. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why is good record-keeping at the triage desk so important for legal safety?

options.A: It stops patients from asking questions about their treatment costs
options.B: It provides a clear record of when the patient arrived and their initial condition
options.C: It guarantees the hospital will win any lawsuit brought by insurance companies
options.D: It allows nurses to avoid writing shift reports at the end of the day

explanation: Clear notes prove exactly when the patient came in and how you cared for them. Good documentation is your best legal shield! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T1#GNS315_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is the main goal of an emergency nursing assessment?

options.A: To establish a comprehensive family medical history
options.B: To diagnose the underlying chronic disease
options.C: To identify and manage life-threatening conditions immediately
options.D: To complete administrative insurance paperwork

explanation: When a patient comes in rushed and critical, your very first duty as a nurse is to find and fix immediate threats to life before anything else. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why does emergency assessment focus on stabilizing the patient before investigating the cause?

options.A: Because nurses are not legally allowed to review past medical records
options.B: Because doctors prefer not to read detailed patient histories
options.C: Because laboratory tests are generally inaccurate in emergency rooms
options.D: Because stabilizing critical threats prevents patient deterioration and death

explanation: Saving a life always comes before finding out why the emergency happened. Keep the patient breathing and stable first! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h1)

question: What does the letter 'D' stand for in the ABCDE primary survey?

options.A: Disability
options.B: Diagnosis
options.C: Dehydration
options.D: Diet

explanation: In the emergency ABCDE framework, D stands for disability, which evaluates basic neurological status. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h2)

question: A patient is brought in bleeding heavily from a leg wound and gasping for air. Following the ABCDE approach, what should you address first?

options.A: Ask the patient for their home address and phone number
options.B: Ensure a patent airway and check breathing
options.C: Clean the leg wound with antiseptic solution
options.D: Document the exact time of the injury in the chart

explanation: Airway and breathing always come first in the ABCDE sequence—even before stopping severe bleeding in circulation! Think A-B-C. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is a classic life-saving action done during the primary survey?

options.A: Applying direct pressure to a severe hemorrhage
options.B: Administering a daily multivitamin tablet
options.C: Explaining hospital discharge policies
options.D: Scheduling a routine physical therapy appointment

explanation: Stopping massive bleeding right away is a critical life-saver to preserve circulation and prevent shock. Great clinical instinct! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h3)

question: Why do nurses often treat life threats at the exact same time they assess the patient in an emergency?

options.A: Because hospital regulations require double documentation for all tasks
options.B: Because doctors prefer to delegate all physical tasks to students
options.C: Because waiting to treat life threats while finishing an assessment can be fatal
options.D: Because nurses have too much free time during shifts

explanation: In critical care, assessment and treatment happen together. A dying patient cannot wait for a slow, complete exam! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h3)

question: When is the right time to start the secondary survey?

options.A: Only after the patient is discharged home
options.B: While the patient is actively in cardiac arrest
options.C: Before checking if the patient has a clear airway
options.D: After the primary survey is done and the patient is stable

explanation: Always make sure immediate life threats in the primary survey are handled before moving on to a detailed secondary survey. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of a head-to-toe secondary survey?

options.A: To determine the financial cost of the hospital stay
options.B: To replace the need for laboratory blood tests entirely
options.C: To check if the patient's clothing is clean and dry
options.D: To discover non-immediate or hidden injuries that the primary survey missed

explanation: Once the patient is safe from dying right away, the secondary survey helps you catch those less obvious bumps, bruises, and fractures. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h4)

question: In the SAMPLE mnemonic, what does the letter 'A' stand for?

options.A: Allergies
options.B: Anxiety
options.C: Activity
options.D: Airway

explanation: Knowing patient allergies is vital before administering any emergency medications. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h5)

question: A patient arrives complaining of severe chest pain. Which mnemonic tool should you use to explore the details of this pain?

options.A: OPQRST
options.B: SAMPLE
options.C: AVPU
options.D: ABCDE

explanation: OPQRST is your best friend for breaking down pain—helping you check its onset, quality, severity, and what makes it better or worse! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary basis for sorting patients at emergency triage?

options.A: Patient's insurance coverage type
options.B: Order of arrival at the hospital
options.C: Severity of illness or injury
options.D: Personal preference of the nurse

explanation: Triage prioritizes care based purely on medical urgency and risk of getting worse, not on who arrived first. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h6)

question: Why is a first-come, first-served system a bad idea in emergency room triage?

options.A: It takes too much time for computer systems to log patients in order
options.B: Patients prefer waiting longer periods for their evaluations
options.C: Hospital administrators legally forbid using arrival times for care
options.D: It could cause a critically ill patient to die in the waiting room while a minor case is seen first

explanation: Triage ensures that limited life-saving resources go straight to the sickest patients first, preventing tragic delays. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h6)

question: How often should an emergency nurse reassess an unstable patient?

options.A: Only once at the very beginning of the shift
options.B: Only when the patient specifically asks for help
options.C: Continuously and frequently throughout the stay
options.D: Just before the patient is discharged home

explanation: Emergency conditions can change in a flash! Frequent, ongoing monitoring keeps you a step ahead. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h7)

question: What is the main danger of failing to do regular reassessments in emergency care?

options.A: Doctors will forget to write discharge prescriptions
options.B: The patient will complain about hospital food quality
options.C: Subtle signs of clinical deterioration may be missed until it is too late
options.D: Insurance companies will refuse to pay the hospital bill

explanation: Regular checks help you catch failing vital signs early, giving you time to step in before things take a turn for the worse. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T2#GNS315_U3_T2_h7)

question: What is the main difference between crowd management and crowd control?

options.A: Crowd management only happens indoors while crowd control is outdoors.
options.B: Crowd management focuses on punishment while crowd control focuses on prevention.
options.C: Crowd management is proactive while crowd control is reactive.
options.D: Crowd management is handled by police while crowd control is for nurses.

explanation: Think of crowd management as planning ahead to keep things smooth and safe. Crowd control is what you do reactively when things get out of hand! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to know about crowd safety during mass gatherings?

options.A: Hospital administrators mandate that all nurses work at concerts and festivals.
options.B: Large crowds often produce sudden medical needs that can overwhelm local hospitals.
options.C: Crowd events are the only places nurses encounter infectious diseases.
options.D: Nurses are legally required to act as event security commanders.

explanation: When thousands of people gather, medical emergencies happen! Nurses play a key role in planning so local hospitals don't get completely overwhelmed. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h1)

question: What is the main danger that causes serious injuries during dense crowd surges?

options.A: Poisoning from contaminated food and water
options.B: Widespread psychological panic and hysteria
options.C: Intentional violence among attendees
options.D: Positional asphyxiation from physical crushing

explanation: It's not just panic—when people get tightly packed together, physical pressure stops them from expanding their chests to breathe properly. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h2)

question: In an emergency, why do people in a crowd often rush back to the exact entrance they used, ignoring other exits?

options.A: Main entrances are always wider and safer during an emergency.
options.B: Security guards physically block all emergency doors.
options.C: People prefer to walk backward rather than explore new areas.
options.D: Herding behavior makes individuals follow familiar routes and mimic others.

explanation: Under stress, human nature kicks in: we tend to stick to what is familiar and copy whatever the person right next to us is doing. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h2)

question: Who should be part of the team planning safety for a big public event?

options.A: Private security guards and catering staff only
options.B: Only the venue owners and local ticket vendors
options.C: Organizers, police, fire services, and healthcare leaders
options.D: Elected politicians and international press agencies

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Keeping a big crowd safe takes everyone—from event planners to healthcare pros and emergency services. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h3)

question: Why is a risk assessment done before holding a mass gathering?

options.A: To reduce ticket prices for attendees
options.B: To eliminate the need for any on-site security personnel
options.C: To identify potential hazards and plan appropriate medical and safety responses
options.D: To guarantee that the event makes a substantial financial profit

explanation: Spotting trouble spots beforehand means we can get medical help and safety measures ready before any emergency strikes. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is the medical and event term for the phase when a crowd is arriving at a venue?

options.A: Ingress
options.B: Triage
options.C: Egress
options.D: Dispersion

explanation: Remember: Ingress means going in (arriving), while egress means exiting (leaving). Easy to mix up, but you've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h4)

question: Why do event planners use zigzag or serpentine queues at entrance gates?

options.A: To slow down entry rates and prevent sudden surges against gates
options.B: To force attendees to purchase merchandise while waiting
options.C: To comply with indoor plumbing regulations
options.D: To make the line look longer than it actually is

explanation: Zigg-zagging lines keep the flow steady and stop impatient crowds from rushing forward and crushing the gates. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which tool do event managers commonly use to watch crowd movement and density in real time?

options.A: Post-event questionnaires
options.B: Weekly weather forecasts
options.C: Closed-circuit television cameras
options.D: Paper registration logs

explanation: CCTV camera feeds give security and medical teams 'eyes everywhere' so they can spot crowd build-ups instantly. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why must on-site spotters communicate with the command center so quickly?

options.A: To allow rapid intervention before minor crowding turns into a crisis
options.B: To ensure ticket sales data is updated every minute
options.C: To prevent performers from starting their show too early
options.D: To coordinate food delivery schedules for vendors

explanation: Spotting a bottleneck early and radioing the team straight away can stop a small crowd crush before it ever starts. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h5)

question: When does an event situation officially become a mass casualty incident (MCI)?

options.A: The number of injured people exceeds available medical resources.
options.B: More than ten people faint from the outdoor heat.
options.C: All electricity to the venue suddenly fails.
options.D: The police decide to shut down the event early.

explanation: An MCI isn't just about a specific number of people—it's when there are simply more injured folks than the medical staff and supplies can handle at once. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why are first aid stations spread out across different areas of a huge venue?

options.A: To prevent attendees from finding the medical tents
options.B: To ensure injured patients can receive treatment quickly without traveling far through crowds
options.C: To ensure all medical supplies are kept in a single warm room
options.D: To reduce the number of nurses needed to staff the event

explanation: Spreading out medical posts means faster help for patients and fewer injured people trying to crawl through heavy crowds. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is a core responsibility of a nurse working at a mass gathering?

options.A: Selling entry tickets at the main gate
options.B: Performing triage and providing initial medical care
options.C: Designing the architectural layout of the stage
options.D: Directing traffic in the venue parking lot

explanation: As a nurse at an event, your superpower here is sorting out who needs help first (triage) and giving quick initial treatment. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h7)

question: At a hot outdoor concert, a nurse notices attendees feeling dizzy, nauseous, and sweating heavily. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Immediately discharge them from the venue without further assessment
options.B: Administer powerful intravenous antibiotics to all affected individuals
options.C: Move them to a shaded cooling area and provide oral rehydration
options.D: Advise them to continue dancing until the concert concludes

explanation: Classic signs of heat exhaustion! Getting them out of the sun and giving fluids right away stops it from turning into heatstroke. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h7)

question: What is the main goal of a post-event debriefing session?

options.A: To celebrate the financial earnings of the event promoters
options.B: To write promotional advertisements for the next gathering
options.C: To punish staff members who made mistakes during the event
options.D: To review operational successes and identify areas needing improvement

explanation: Debriefs are all about learning. The team looks at what went well and what can be improved for the next big event. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h8)

question: Why do planners analyze medical logs and hospital transport times after an event ends?

options.A: To calculate the exact profit margin of the food vendors
options.B: To determine which medical staff members should receive a salary cut
options.C: To evaluate the effectiveness of the medical response and refine future planning
options.D: To verify that all attendees purchased official merchandise

explanation: Looking at medical records helps planners figure out if they had enough nurses, supplies, or ambulances, making future events even safer. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T3#GNS315_U3_T3_h8)

question: What is the main reason we use the ABCDEF protocol in emergency care?

options.A: To document nursing care for legal cover
options.B: To figure out the final medical diagnosis
options.C: To replace the need for lab tests
options.D: To find and treat life-threatening problems step-by-step

explanation: You've got this! The ABCDEF guide helps healthcare teams tackle the scariest, most immediate life threats first so nothing gets missed. Great job thinking like an emergency nurse! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h1)

question: If a patient is stable and suddenly starts getting worse during an ABCDEF check, what should the team do right away?

options.A: Rush the patient to the operating theatre
options.B: Go straight back to step A and check the airway again
options.C: Finish the rest of the protocol steps first
options.D: Wait at the bedside for the doctor to arrive

explanation: Spot on! If a patient takes a turn for the worse, always cycle right back to the beginning (Airway) to catch any new breathing or airway trouble. Excellent clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why is checking the airway always the very first step in emergency care?

options.A: Hospital rules strictly say airway first
options.B: It keeps the patient from talking too much
options.C: A blocked airway can cause death in minutes
options.D: It is the easiest thing to do in a busy ward

explanation: Spot on! Without a clear airway, oxygen can't reach the lungs, leading to brain death and cardiac arrest very fast. Airway always comes first! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h2)

question: An unconscious accident victim is brought in with heavy bleeding in their mouth. What is your very first nursing action?

options.A: Lay them flat on their back without neck support
options.B: Suction the airway while keeping the neck safely supported
options.C: Give oral pain meds to keep them calm
options.D: Send them straight for a chest X-ray

explanation: Brilliant! Clearing the mouth clears the airway, but always remember to protect that vulnerable neck from spinal injury at the same time. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h2)

question: What is a major sign that a patient is struggling to breathe during an emergency check?

options.A: A calm, relaxed face
options.B: Warm, dry skin with pink nail beds
options.C: A steady pulse of 72 beats per minute
options.D: Working hard to breathe and low oxygen saturation

explanation: You nailed it! When a patient is visibly struggling for breath and their oxygen levels drop, it's a clear warning sign that their breathing needs urgent help. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why must a nurse pull back the clothes and actually look at the patient's bare chest during a breathing assessment?

options.A: To listen for tummy sounds in the chest
options.B: To check the exact skin temperature
options.C: To check for chest symmetry, injuries, and odd movements
options.D: To get the skin ready for ECG stickers

explanation: Exactly! Looking closely helps you spot uneven chest rise, hidden wounds, or flail segments that make breathing difficult. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is the fastest, most effective way to stop severe bleeding on a patient's arm or leg?

options.A: Give them water to drink to replace lost blood
options.B: Lift the legs up high
options.C: Apply direct pressure or a tourniquet
options.D: Apply ice packs directly to the wound

explanation: Well done! Direct pressure or a tourniquet squeezes those bleeding vessels shut and stops dangerous blood loss fast. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h4)

question: A patient in the ER has a fast heart rate, cool sweaty skin, and slow capillary refill. What do these signs tell you?

options.A: They are simply recovering from light exercise
options.B: The brain and heart are getting plenty of oxygen
options.C: Poor blood flow and possible shock
options.D: The nervous system is just overactive

explanation: Spot on! The body pulls blood away from the skin to protect vital organs like the heart and brain when blood volume is low. Classic signs of shock! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h4)

question: In the quick AVPU neurological check scale, what does the letter 'V' stand for?

options.A: Venous pressure
options.B: Verbal response
options.C: Visual acuity
options.D: Ventilation rate

explanation: You got it! V stands for verbal—meaning the patient reacts or speaks when you talk to them. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h5)

question: An ER patient is confused, pale, and sleepy. You check their blood sugar and find it is very low at 2.2 mmol/L. What is likely going on?

options.A: The confusion and sleepiness are likely caused by low blood sugar
options.B: They need emergency brain surgery right away
options.C: Their mental state is completely normal for their age
options.D: They have a permanent spinal cord injury

explanation: Brilliant! The brain runs on glucose. When sugar drops too low, confusion sets in—and it usually clears up quickly once sugar is given. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is a major danger when you completely strip off a trauma patient's clothing during the 'Exposure' step?

options.A: Sudden spikes in high blood pressure
options.B: Sudden waking up from unconsciousness
options.C: Bad allergic reactions to hospital sheets
options.D: Hypothermia and rapid body heat loss

explanation: Spot on! Cold ER rooms can drop a patient's core temperature fast, and cold blood doesn't clot properly. Always protect their warmth! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h6)

question: How should a nurse balance checking a patient's naked skin for injuries while keeping them warm during step 'E'?

options.A: Avoid taking off any clothes at all to keep them warm
options.B: Turn off all room fans to heat up the room
options.C: Leave the patient completely naked for hours to watch their skin
options.D: Uncover body parts briefly to check them, then cover the patient with warm blankets

explanation: You got it! Quick, targeted checks followed by covering them right back up lets you spot injuries without freezing the patient. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h6)

question: Aside from taking baseline vital signs, what modern addition does the letter 'F' often stand for in emergency protocols?

options.A: Family presence
options.B: Fluid restriction
options.C: Fast intubation
options.D: Fracture casting

explanation: Excellent! Modern emergency care recognizes that having loved ones nearby helps reduce anxiety and supports the patient through a crisis. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is the main job of the support nurse when family members are allowed in the room during an active emergency resuscitation?

options.A: To write down every single drug given by the doctor
options.B: To chase all visitors out of the hospital building
options.C: To do chest compressions if the main rescuer gets tired
options.D: To explain procedures, offer comfort, and answer the family's questions

explanation: Spot on! Having a dedicated nurse look after the family keeps them informed and calm, leaving the rest of the team free to focus fully on saving the patient. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T4#GNS315_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is the main goal of giving artificial respiration?

options.A: To lower body temperature
options.B: To stimulate heart contractions
options.C: To increase blood pressure
options.D: To maintain adequate gas exchange

explanation: You've got this! Artificial respiration simply steps in to deliver fresh oxygen and blow off carbon dioxide when a patient's natural breathing isn't enough. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h1)

question: How does positive pressure ventilation differ from how we normally breathe?

options.A: It relies entirely on cellular metabolism
options.B: It uses the diaphragm instead of external machinery
options.C: It pushes air into the lungs instead of creating negative pressure
options.D: It only removes carbon dioxide without giving oxygen

explanation: Think of normal breathing like pulling air in by expanding your chest (negative pressure). Machines or manual bags do the opposite—they gently push air right in! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which of these is a late sign that a patient is running low on oxygen in their blood?

options.A: Hypertension
options.B: Cyanosis
options.C: Tachycardia
options.D: Sweating

explanation: Cyanosis—that bluish tint to the lips and skin—shows up when oxygen levels have been dropping for a bit. It's a classic clinical cue to act fast! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h2)

question: Your patient looks drowsy, confused, and is working hard just to breathe using their neck muscles. What is your best next step?

options.A: Apply a standard nasal cannula with low flow
options.B: Prepare for immediate respiratory support
options.C: Encourage the patient to sleep it off
options.D: Wait for laboratory blood test results

explanation: When a patient is this exhausted and using accessory muscles, they are tiring out fast. Getting respiratory support ready right away can save their life! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is the everyday clinical nickname for a bag-valve-mask device?

options.A: Suction catheter
options.B: Venturi mask
options.C: Ambu bag
options.D: Nebulizer

explanation: You will hear nurses and doctors call this the 'Ambu bag' all the time on the ward. It's your best friend in an emergency! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h3)

question: Why shouldn't you squeeze a manual resuscitator bag way too hard during ventilation?

options.A: It causes the oxygen tank to explode
options.B: It instantly damages the heart muscle
options.C: It prevents carbon dioxide from leaving the room
options.D: It can force air into the stomach and cause vomiting

explanation: Squeezing too hard opens up the pathway to the stomach. Filling the stomach with air is a quick ticket to vomiting and aspiration—definitely something we want to avoid! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h3)

question: What is the main job of the tiny balloon cuff on an endotracheal tube?

options.A: To pump oxygen automatically into the lungs
options.B: To filter dust from incoming room air
options.C: To measure the patient's blood pressure
options.D: To secure the tube in place and prevent aspiration

explanation: Inflating that little cuff creates a gentle seal inside the windpipe. It keeps the tube firmly in position and blocks stomach contents from slipping into the lungs. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is the most reliable way to immediately check if an endotracheal tube is placed correctly?

options.A: Measuring abdominal girth with a tape
options.B: Listening for equal breath sounds and checking carbon dioxide levels
options.C: Checking the color of the patient's fingernails
options.D: Feeling the pulse rate on the wrist

explanation: Always listen to both sides of the chest and check for exhaled carbon dioxide. This guarantees the tube is safely in the lungs, not accidentally in the stomach! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h4)

question: Which of these is a key nursing duty to help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?

options.A: Giving strong antibiotics to every intubated patient
options.B: Keeping the head of the bed completely flat
options.C: Changing the ventilator machine every hour
options.D: Performing regular oral care with antiseptic solutions

explanation: Mouth hygiene is huge! Keeping the mouth clean stops nasty bacteria from multiplying and sliding down into the lungs. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why should the head of a patient's bed be kept elevated while they are on a mechanical ventilator?

options.A: To reduce the risk of gastric contents entering the lungs
options.B: To increase the speed of the ventilator motor
options.C: To help the nurse chart more comfortably
options.D: To make it easier for visitors to see the patient's face

explanation: Gravity is on our side when the bed is raised. It keeps stomach acid and food where they belong—down in the stomach! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is your safest immediate action if a mechanical ventilator suddenly stops working and you don't know why?

options.A: Disconnect the patient and ventilate manually with an Ambu bag
options.B: Turn off the machine and wait for a doctor to arrive
options.C: Increase the oxygen flow rate on the wall meter
options.D: Pull out the endotracheal tube immediately

explanation: Machines can glitch, but your patient needs oxygen right now. Grab the Ambu bag and ventilate manually while you call for help! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h6)

question: A high-pressure ventilator alarm starts going off. What is the most common culprit?

options.A: Secretions or a kink in the breathing tube
options.B: An empty oxygen tank outside the room
options.C: A loose connection somewhere in the plastic tubing
options.D: The patient breathing too slowly on their own

explanation: When a tube gets blocked by thick mucus or a bite, the machine has to push harder, setting off that high-pressure alarm. Check the tubing first! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h6)

question: In respiratory care, what does the term 'weaning' mean?

options.A: Lowering the room temperature to cool the patient
options.B: Gradually transitioning the patient back to spontaneous breathing
options.C: Stopping nutrition support to rest the stomach
options.D: Removing all medications from the patient's intravenous line

explanation: Weaning is like taking off the training wheels. As the patient gets stronger, we slowly reduce machine support so they can breathe on their own again. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h7)

question: Which sign might tell you that a patient is struggling during a ventilator weaning trial?

options.A: Sweating and an increasing heart rate
options.B: Asking for a glass of cold water
options.C: Calm facial expression and steady sleep
options.D: Lower blood pressure and normal breathing

explanation: If a patient breaks out in a sweat (diaphoresis) and their heart rate spikes, it's a clear distress signal telling us the breathing workload is still too heavy for them. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T5#GNS315_U3_T5_h7)

question: What is the main job of a mechanical ventilator in the hospital ward?

options.A: To support or replace spontaneous breathing
options.B: To permanently eliminate the need for oxygen therapy
options.C: To cure underlying pulmonary infections
options.D: To lower systemic blood pressure safely

explanation: Think of the ventilator as an extra pair of lungs for patients who are too tired or sick to breathe well on their own. It takes over or helps out until they recover! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why would a patient who took a severe drug overdose be put on a mechanical ventilator?

options.A: Reversal of central nervous system toxicity
options.B: Immediate elimination of the drug from the lungs
options.C: Airway protection and respiratory support
options.D: Prevention of future drug dependency

explanation: When someone is deeply unconscious from an overdose, their body forgets to protect its own airway. The ventilator keeps them breathing safely and stops any spit or vomit from entering their lungs. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which ventilator mode gives a set volume when the patient tries to breathe, but also guarantees a minimum backup rate if they get too tired?

options.A: Control mode
options.B: Assist-Control mode
options.C: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
options.D: Pressure Support mode

explanation: In Assist-Control mode, the machine is always watching: if the patient breathes, the machine helps out with a full breath. If the patient stops trying, the machine's timer steps in to breathe for them! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h2)

question: How does SIMV (Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation) differ from Assist-Control mode?

options.A: SIMV delivers breaths only when the patient makes zero respiratory effort
options.B: SIMV allows spontaneous breaths between mandatory machine breaths without extra volume support
options.C: SIMV is only used for patients who are paralyzed or heavily sedated
options.D: SIMV completely controls every single breath the patient takes without exception

explanation: SIMV gives the patient a bit of freedom! The machine gives scheduled breaths, but in between those, the patient can take their own natural breaths without the machine forcing extra air. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h2)

question: When setting up a ventilator for an adult patient, which measurement is used to calculate the starting tidal volume?

options.A: Actual admission weight
options.B: Height plus blood pressure
options.C: Total body surface area
options.D: Ideal body weight

explanation: Lung size depends on a person's skeletal frame and height, not extra body fat. That's why we use ideal body weight to avoid overinflating their lungs! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h3)

question: When a patient is newly connected to a ventilator, what is the most common starting PEEP (Positive End-Expiratory Pressure) setting used to keep small air sacs open?

options.A: 20 cmH2O
options.B: 5 cmH2O
options.C: 0 cmH2O
options.D: 50 cmH2O

explanation: A baseline PEEP of 5 cmH2O acts like a gentle cushion at the end of each breath, stopping tiny air sacs (alveoli) from collapsing so breathing stays easier. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h3)

question: What is the most common cause of a high-pressure ventilator alarm?

options.A: A sudden massive air leak in the circuit
options.B: The patient has stopped breathing completely
options.C: Obstruction, coughing, or tube kinking
options.D: Disconnection of the ventilator tubing

explanation: A high-pressure alarm means the machine is struggling to push air in because something is blocking the path—like thick mucus, the patient biting the tube, or a kink in the tubing. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the very first thing you should do as a nurse when a ventilator alarm sounds?

options.A: Check the patient directly and assess circuit connections
options.B: Call the physician immediately to request new settings
options.C: Silence the alarm permanently at the main console
options.D: Increase the oxygen percentage to 100 percent

explanation: Always check the human before the machine! Walk straight to the bedside to make sure the patient is safe and the breathing tube hasn't popped loose. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h4)

question: To prevent lung infections in a patient on a ventilator, what angle should the head of their bed be elevated?

options.A: 90 degrees upright
options.B: 0 to 10 degrees
options.C: 60 to 75 degrees
options.D: 30 to 45 degrees

explanation: Keeping the bed raised between 30 and 45 degrees uses gravity to stop oral secretions and stomach contents from sliding down into the lungs. Simple and life-saving! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why should you suction a patient's breathing tube based on clinical need rather than a strict routine schedule?

options.A: Suctioning can cause mucosal trauma, bleeding, and oxygen desaturation
options.B: Mucus production completely stops once a patient is intubated
options.C: Strict schedules increase the cost of disposable suction catheters
options.D: Scheduled suctioning causes the ventilator to malfunction

explanation: Suctioning is rough on the delicate lining of the windpipe and temporarily steals oxygen. We only do it when we actually hear or see secretions, protecting our patient from unnecessary harm. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which complication happens when high ventilator pressures cause tiny air sacs to rupture and air leaks into the chest cavity?

options.A: Pulmonary edema
options.B: Atelectasis
options.C: Pneumothorax
options.D: Pleural effusion

explanation: Too much pressure can pop overstretched alveoli, letting air leak into the space around the lung and causing it to collapse (a pneumothorax). [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h6)

question: Why can high levels of positive pressure ventilation sometimes cause a patient's blood pressure to drop?

options.A: It increases the heart rate so high that filling time is eliminated
options.B: It increases pressure inside the chest, which reduces blood return to the heart
options.C: It forces fluid directly out of the vascular system into the tissues
options.D: It directly causes systemic vasodilation through chemical release

explanation: Think of the chest as a closed box. Pumping too much air in crowds the major veins, making it harder for blood to flow back to the heart, which dips the blood pressure. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h6)

question: What test is commonly used to check if a patient is strong enough to come off mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Arterial blood gas challenge
options.B: Continuous positive pressure test
options.C: Pulmonary function spirometry
options.D: Spontaneous breathing trial

explanation: A spontaneous breathing trial lets the patient test-drive their own lungs with very little machine help for a short period to see if they are ready to breathe entirely on their own. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h7)

question: During a weaning trial, which sign tells you that the patient is struggling and needs ventilator support put back on?

options.A: A stable heart rate of 80 beats per minute
options.B: Use of accessory muscles and heavy sweating
options.C: An oxygen saturation level remaining at 96 percent
options.D: Calm restfulness with normal breathing rhythm

explanation: If you see a patient sweating, working hard with their neck and chest muscles, and breathing frantically, their muscles are exhausted. It's time to put the machine back on support! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T6#GNS315_U3_T6_h7)

question: What is the main goal of giving CPR to a patient?

options.A: To clear a blocked airway using forced abdominal thrusts
options.B: To cure the underlying cause of a sudden heart attack
options.C: To manually circulate oxygenated blood to vital organs
options.D: To restart a stopped heart using manual electric shocks

explanation: You're doing great! Remember that CPR doesn't usually restart the heart on its own. Instead, your hands act as a pump to keep oxygen flowing to the brain and heart until help arrives. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why do we need to start CPR immediately when someone goes into cardiac arrest?

options.A: The lungs will collapse permanently within thirty seconds
options.B: Body temperature drops too fast for resuscitation to work
options.C: Brain damage begins within minutes due to lack of oxygen
options.D: Blood clots will instantly form in all major blood vessels

explanation: Spot on! When the heart stops, oxygen stops reaching the brain right away. Acting fast prevents permanent damage and saves lives. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h1)

question: In the out-of-hospital chain of survival, what comes right after recognizing the emergency and calling for help?

options.A: Post-resuscitation care
options.B: Early CPR
options.C: Early defibrillation
options.D: Advanced life support

explanation: You've got this! After calling for help, getting hands on the chest for early CPR is the next vital step to keep blood moving. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h2)

question: Why are all the steps in the chain of survival equally important?

options.A: Advanced drugs cannot be given before every step is completed
options.B: Each step must be performed by the exact same healthcare provider
options.C: Defibrillation will fail if the patient is not in a hospital bed
options.D: A failure in any single step drastically lowers overall survival odds

explanation: Think of it like a real chain—if one link breaks, the whole thing fails! Every single step helps give the patient the best fighting chance. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h2)

question: When checking if an unresponsive patient is breathing normally, what is the maximum time a nurse should spend on this?

options.A: One minute
options.B: Thirty seconds
options.C: Ten seconds
options.D: Two minutes

explanation: Nice and quick! We check for breathing and a pulse at the same time, but we never want to waste precious seconds—keep it under 10 seconds so compressions aren't delayed. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h3)

question: If an unresponsive patient is taking slow, gasping, irregular breaths, how should a nurse respond?

options.A: As an indication to wait for natural breathing to stabilize
options.B: As a sign that the patient is recovering normal oxygen levels
options.C: As agonal respirations requiring immediate start of CPR
options.D: As proof that the airway is clear and no further action is needed

explanation: Don't let those gasps fool you! Agonal gasps are just a reflex when the heart stops. Treat them as cardiac arrest and start CPR right away. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h3)

question: How deep should your chest compressions be when doing high-quality CPR on an adult?

options.A: Five centimeters minimum
options.B: One-half inch maximum
options.C: At least two inches
options.D: Exactly four inches

explanation: You're doing great. To squeeze that heart enough to push blood out, you need to press down at least two inches deep! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h4)

question: You notice a student nurse leaning heavily on the patient's chest between chest compressions. What advice should you give?

options.A: Bend your elbows to reduce pressure on the patient's ribs
options.B: Allow full chest recoil so the heart can refill with blood
options.C: Stop compressions completely and check for a carotid pulse
options.D: Increase the speed to one hundred fifty pushes per minute

explanation: Leaning is a common mistake! Remind them to let the chest spring all the way back up so the heart chambers can refill with fresh blood for the next push. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h4)

question: Which airway opening technique should you use if you suspect a neck injury in a cardiac arrest patient?

options.A: Lateral recovery position
options.B: Jaw-thrust maneuver
options.C: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver
options.D: Neck-hyperextension technique

explanation: Safety first! The jaw-thrust lets you open the airway without bending or moving the neck, keeping the cervical spine safe in trauma cases. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why is it dangerous to give rescue breaths too fast or with too much force?

options.A: It can force air into the stomach and lead to vomiting
options.B: It immediately collapses both lungs due to high pressure
options.C: It causes the patient's heart rate to drop dangerously low
options.D: It forces blood backward into the jugular veins

explanation: Easy does it with breaths! Blowing too hard opens up the stomach instead of the lungs, which can cause the patient to vomit and complicate things. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of delivering a shock with an Automated External Defibrillator (AED)?

options.A: To warm up cold heart muscle tissue after a cardiac arrest
options.B: To interrupt a chaotic heart rhythm and let it reset
options.C: To measure the exact blood pressure inside the ventricles
options.D: To restart a completely flat heart line during asystole

explanation: Think of the AED as a reset button! It momentarily stuns a wildly quivering heart so the heart's natural pacemaker can take back control. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h6)

question: Why must everyone step back and not touch the patient while the AED is analyzing or shocking?

options.A: Movement can interfere with rhythm analysis or cause accidental shocks
options.B: Rescuers will catch the electrical current and stop breathing
options.C: The physical vibration of standing nearby stops the machine
options.D: The AED machine requires complete silence to function properly

explanation: Safety rule number one during an AED check: clear everybody! Movement tricks the machine's rhythm reader and can even shock the person touching the patient. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h6)

question: Which medication is commonly given during cardiac arrest to boost blood flow to the heart and brain?

options.A: Epinephrine
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Digoxin
options.D: Warfarin

explanation: You'll see epinephrine used often in codes! It acts as a powerful vasoconstrictor to push blood where it's needed most during resuscitation. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h7)

question: How does placing an advanced breathing tube (like an endotracheal tube) change how CPR is performed?

options.A: Rescuers can give continuous compressions without pausing for breaths
options.B: Medications can only be given directly through the breathing tube
options.C: Chest compressions are stopped entirely while artificial breaths are given
options.D: Defibrillation pads are no longer needed once the tube is inserted

explanation: Once the tube is secured, teamwork gets easier—compressors can keep pushing without stopping to give breaths every few seconds! [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is a very common physical injury that happens even during proper, high-quality chest compressions?

options.A: Skull fracture
options.B: Spinal dislocation
options.C: Rib fractures
options.D: Lung collapse

explanation: Don't be alarmed if you feel a crack! Pushing hard enough to save a life often causes minor rib or sternum fractures—saving the life comes first. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h8)

question: What is the main goal of targeted temperature management after a patient is successfully revived?

options.A: To prevent the development of blood clots in the legs
options.B: To protect the brain from injury caused by lack of oxygen
options.C: To lower the heart rate back down to normal resting levels
options.D: To stop the patient from shivering and burning calories

explanation: Cooling the body down slows down brain activity, giving injured brain cells a much better chance to recover after a cardiac arrest. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h8)

question: Which document tells a nurse NOT to start CPR on an unresponsive patient?

options.A: A general medical insurance policy
options.B: A valid do-not-resuscitate order
options.C: A verbal request from a distant relative
options.D: A standard hospital admission form

explanation: Always respect patient wishes! A signed and valid Do-Not-Resuscitate (DNR) order or advance directive legally stops us from initiating CPR. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h9)

question: What should you do if a patient is in cardiac arrest and you cannot find their advance directive papers right away?

options.A: Begin CPR immediately because life preservation is the priority
options.B: Withhold treatment until hospital security investigates the case
options.C: Ask the physician on duty to sign an emergency DNR form
options.D: Wait up to thirty minutes for family members to bring paperwork

explanation: When in doubt, save a life! If official paperwork isn't right in front of you, your duty is to start CPR immediately. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T7#GNS315_U3_T7_h9)

question: What is the main goal of a medical evacuation (medevac)?

options.A: To move a patient to a facility with higher-level care
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of hospital treatment
options.C: To clear crowded hospital beds for new admissions
options.D: To provide permanent long-term rehabilitation therapy

explanation: Medevac is all about bridging the gap! It safely transports patients from places with limited resources to specialized centers where they can get the exact treatment they need. [learn more](GNS315_U3_T8#GNS315_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why is time such a critical factor during an emergency medevac?

options.A: Delays significantly worsen survival rates in severe trauma
options.B: Receiving doctors finish their shifts at fixed times
options.C: Transport vehicles have strict hourly rental limits
