options.B: It replaces the need for community education and local drills
options.C: It guarantees that natural hazards will completely miss the country
options.D: It ensures that different groups do not duplicate efforts and waste resources

explanation: Brilliant! Sharing information and working hand-in-hand prevents confusion and keeps help running smoothly. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T11#GNS315_U5_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of disaster monitoring in nursing?

options.A: Writing historical books about past weather events
options.B: Systematically collecting and analyzing data during crises
options.C: Punishing facilities that fail to prepare for emergencies
options.D: Replacing the role of physicians in emergency rooms

explanation: Disaster monitoring is all about watching, gathering, and studying information so healthcare workers can respond effectively to emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h1)

question: How does a nurse's role change during disaster monitoring compared to routine bedside care?

options.A: The focus shifts toward population health and community-wide safety
options.B: Nurses stop caring for individual patients entirely
options.C: Administrative paperwork replaces all hands-on nursing duties
options.D: Clinical assessment skills are no longer needed in the field

explanation: While bedside care focuses on one patient at a time, disaster monitoring broadens the nurse's view to entire communities and resource tracking. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which phase of disaster monitoring involves watching weather patterns and community vulnerabilities before an event hits?

options.A: Post-disaster phase
options.B: Recovery-only phase
options.C: Pre-disaster phase
options.D: Trans-disaster phase

explanation: The pre-disaster phase focuses on preparation, tracking risks, and looking at weather or health data before a crisis occurs. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is a nurse primarily monitoring during the trans-disaster phase?

options.A: Historical trends of past earthquakes over fifty years
options.B: Routine annual budget reports for hospital supplies
options.C: Real-time casualties, bed availability, and active environmental hazards
options.D: Long-term economic recovery and rebuilding costs

explanation: The trans-disaster phase happens right during the event, requiring immediate tracking of injuries, hospital space, and ongoing dangers. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is the main function of an early warning system in a disaster context?

options.A: Calculating the financial cost of destroyed property
options.B: Treating injuries after a building collapses
options.C: Detecting threats early before they cause widespread harm
options.D: Punishing individuals who ignore safety rules

explanation: Early warning systems use technology and data to spot danger ahead of time so people can prepare and evacuate. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h3)

question: A nurse notices a sudden cluster of patients arriving with severe vomiting and diarrhea from the same neighborhood. What action best reflects hazard identification?

options.A: Asking the hospital finance department to buy more IV fluids
options.B: Waiting until next week to see if more people show up at the clinic
options.C: Reporting the unusual disease pattern to public health authorities immediately
options.D: Telling the patients it is just a normal stomach flu and sending them home

explanation: Spotting unusual symptom clusters and alerting authorities helps catch outbreaks early before they turn into major disasters. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does syndromic surveillance primarily track during a health emergency?

options.A: Only confirmed laboratory cases of rare tropical diseases
options.B: Hospital staff attendance records during a night shift
options.C: Groups of symptoms before laboratory tests are confirmed
options.D: The exact financial cost of medical equipment used

explanation: Syndromic surveillance watches symptom patterns early on, allowing teams to act fast without waiting for slow lab test results. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h4)

question: Why is using standardized definitions for injuries and symptoms crucial during a disaster?

options.A: It stops patients from complaining about long waiting times
options.B: It allows doctors to avoid writing detailed patient progress notes
options.C: It reduces the total number of patients admitted to the hospital
options.D: It ensures that data collected from different clinics can be accurately combined

explanation: When everyone uses the same definitions, health authorities can trust the combined numbers from multiple clinics and hospitals. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following is an example of resource tracking during a disaster?

options.A: Counting how many hours of sleep nurses got last night
options.B: Interviewing community leaders about past local floods
options.C: Predicting what the weather will look like next month
options.D: Monitoring available hospital beds and oxygen tank supplies

explanation: Resource tracking keeps an active count of vital physical items and space needed to care for incoming patients. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is a major risk of failing to monitor resource logistics actively during a crisis?

options.A: Patients recovering much faster than expected
options.B: Lower hospital electricity bills for the month
options.C: Too many medical supplies cluttering the hallways
options.D: Unexpected stockouts that halt life-saving treatments

explanation: Without active tracking, hospitals run out of critical items like oxygen or IV fluids right when demand is highest. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h5)

question: What communication tool helps nurses pass structured and concise patient or situation data during a crisis?

options.A: Casual text messages sent without checking details
options.B: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation)
options.C: Complex medical research articles from foreign journals
options.D: Long narrative diary entries written at the end of the shift

explanation: SBAR gives healthcare workers a quick, organized way to share essential facts without wasting time during emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why is it important to avoid heavy clinical jargon when reporting disaster monitoring data to non-medical coordinators?

options.A: To ensure disaster coordinators understand the message and act on it quickly
options.B: To make the report look less professional and more casual
options.C: Because clinical terms are illegal to use outside of hospital buildings
options.D: Because non-medical personnel are not allowed to hear health statistics

explanation: Clear, plain language prevents dangerous misunderstandings between health workers and municipal response teams. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h6)

question: What ethical balance must nurses maintain while collecting data during a disaster?

options.A: Balancing hospital profits with the cost of medical textbooks
options.B: Balancing nursing working hours with physician holiday schedules
options.C: Balancing public health surveillance needs with patient privacy and confidentiality
options.D: Balancing local laws with international travel restrictions

explanation: Nurses must track outbreaks to protect the public while still respecting each patient's right to private medical information. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following actions is NOT legally or ethically acceptable when monitoring a public health crisis?

options.A: Ensuring fair distribution of available medical supplies to all patients
options.B: Tracking the total number of cholera cases admitted to the ward
options.C: Reporting anonymous symptom data to the local ministry of health
options.D: Broadcasting identifiable personal details of patients on public social media

explanation: Sharing private patient names and identifying details publicly violates confidentiality laws and ethical nursing standards. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of a post-disaster debriefing or hot wash session?

options.A: Calculating annual bonuses for hospital administrators
options.B: Analyzing what went well and where emergency processes failed
options.C: Assigning blame to individual nurses who made mistakes
options.D: Destroying all medical records from the disaster period

explanation: Debriefings review the response objectively so the healthcare team can learn and improve for future emergencies. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h8)

question: How do post-disaster evaluation data directly benefit future community health responses?

options.A: By guiding updates to emergency action plans and preparedness training
options.B: By proving that disasters can be completely prevented from ever happening
options.C: By reducing the number of nurses required on future hospital shifts
options.D: By eliminating the need for any future weather monitoring equipment

explanation: Learning from past mistakes allows hospitals to update their disaster plans and train staff more effectively for next time. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h8)

question: What is the main goal of search and rescue operations when a disaster hits?

options.A: Clear debris and rebuild destroyed public infrastructure
options.B: Distribute food and clean water to affected communities
options.C: Locate, extricate, and deliver victims to medical care
options.D: Provide long-term rehabilitation for displaced families

explanation: You've got this! Search and rescue is simply about finding those who are missing, getting them out safely, and handing them over for medical treatment. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h1)

question: Why do nurses working in disaster zones need to understand how search and rescue operations work?

options.A: Healthcare delivery often starts right at the edge of the rescue zone
options.B: Nurses are required to operate heavy machinery during building collapses
options.C: Medical staff must personally enter unstable structures to find victims
options.D: Hospital administrators mandate that nurses lead field rescue teams

explanation: Spot on! Medical care doesn't wait until the patient reaches a hospital; it begins the moment they are pulled out, right at the boundary of the danger zone. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which phase of a rescue operation involves sweeping the disaster area to find where victims are trapped?

options.A: Stabilization
options.B: Localization
options.C: Extrication
options.D: Evacuation

explanation: Think of localization as the mapping and finding stage. Teams use tools, dogs, and visual sweeps to spot exactly where trapped people are. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h2)

question: Why must rescue workers stabilize a victim before moving them to a hospital?

options.A: To address life-threatening injuries and prevent deterioration during transport
options.B: To ensure the rescue team gets enough rest before the next mission
options.C: To reduce the total paperwork required by the receiving hospital staff
options.D: To identify the personal belongings and insurance status of the patient

explanation: Brilliant! Stabilizing stops immediate threats like severe bleeding so the patient can survive the bumpy journey to the hospital. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h2)

question: Where do medical teams usually set up to treat victims rescued from a disaster site?

options.A: Inside the headquarters office miles away from the disaster area
options.B: Deep inside the collapsed building right next to the trapped victims
options.C: At the final destination tertiary hospital only
options.D: At forward medical posts near the safe edge of the hazard zone

explanation: You're doing great! Setting up close to the hazard zone means rescued victims get help instantly, without putting the medical team right in harm's way. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h3)

question: A rescue team is about to free a trapped miner whose legs were under rubble for hours. What critical medical step must nurses prepare for?

options.A: Preparing the patient for immediate general anesthesia in the field
options.B: Withholding all fluids to prevent severe pulmonary edema
options.C: Applying a tight tourniquet to every limb before any movement starts
options.D: Administering large volumes of intravenous fluids to prevent kidney failure

explanation: Spot on! When trapped limbs are freed, toxins rush into the bloodstream. IV fluids help flush these out before they can shut down the kidneys. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h3)

question: What does the 'R' stand for in the START triage system used during disasters?

options.A: Rapid
options.B: Resuscitation
options.C: Recovery
options.D: Respiratory

explanation: START stands for Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment, designed for fast categorization in mass casualty incidents. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h4)

question: Why must nurses keep reassessing patients who have already been sorted into a triage category?

options.A: Rescue teams need to change patient names frequently
options.B: Color tags often fall off in wet weather conditions
options.C: Hospital admission clerks require updated paperwork every hour
options.D: A patient's condition can rapidly deteriorate over time

explanation: Exactly! Injuries can hide beneath the surface, meaning a patient who looks stable now could crash and need urgent help a few minutes later. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT standard personal protective equipment (PPE) for a field rescuer?

options.A: High-visibility vest
options.B: Sterile surgical gown
options.C: Hard hat
options.D: Steel-toed boots

explanation: You nailed it. Surgical gowns belong in the operating theatre, not out in the mud and rubble where hard hats and boots keep you safe! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h5)

question: Why is personal safety emphasized as the top priority for search and rescue workers?

options.A: Rescue equipment is too expensive to risk losing in a collapse
options.B: Injured rescuers drain resources and create extra victims for the team
options.C: Hospital insurance policies do not cover field injuries
options.D: Rescuers are legally forbidden from receiving medical treatment

explanation: Well thought out! If a rescuer gets hurt, everyone has to stop what they're doing to save them, which puts the whole mission in jeopardy. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h5)

question: What does the 'C' stand for in the ABCDE pre-hospital emergency care framework?

options.A: Consciousness
options.B: Cardiac
options.C: Collapse
options.D: Circulation

explanation: In emergency trauma care, C stands for Circulation, focusing on checking pulses and stopping severe bleeding. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why is preventing hypothermia so important when stabilizing a trauma victim?

options.A: Standard rescue stretchers only function properly in warm weather
options.B: Hypothermia causes patients to become overly aggressive with staff
options.C: Warm patients require fewer intravenous fluids during transport
options.D: Cold exposure worsens blood clotting problems and increases mortality

explanation: You're doing awesome. Trauma patients lose body heat fast, and cold temperatures stop blood from clotting properly, making bleeding much harder to control. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h6)

question: When are helicopter or boat transport methods most necessary during a disaster evacuation?

options.A: When floods, landslides, or collapsed bridges block traditional roads
options.B: When the patient has a minor injury and lives next to a hospital
options.C: When hospital emergency rooms are completely empty
options.D: When ground ambulances are running low on diesel fuel only

explanation: Spot on! When roads are completely impassable due to natural disasters, air and water transport are the only ways out. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h7)

question: Why is securing a patient onto a rigid spine board or basket stretcher essential during transport?

options.A: It prevents worsening of potential spinal cord injuries over rough terrain
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will fall into a deep sleep
options.C: It allows the driver to travel at maximum speed without slowing down
options.D: It eliminates the need for any vital sign monitoring during the journey

explanation: Brilliant! Rigid boards keep the spine straight and steady, protecting the patient from paralysis during bumpy evacuation rides. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of debriefing sessions for rescue personnel after an operation?

options.A: To punish team members who made minor mistakes during the rescue
options.B: To process emotional experiences and access mental health support
options.C: To calculate financial overtime pay and distribute hazard allowances
options.D: To conduct written examinations on disaster rescue theory

explanation: You've got this! Debriefings give rescue workers a safe space to talk through the heavy stress and trauma they witnessed on the job. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h8)

question: What is the best way for a nurse to provide psychological first aid to a disaster victim?

options.A: Encouraging the victim to forget the event and focus on rebuilding
options.B: Offering a calm presence and active listening without false promises
options.C: Leaving the victim alone immediately so they can process their grief
options.D: Telling the victim that everything will quickly return to normal

explanation: Wonderful! Psychological first aid is all about being present, listening patiently, and supporting them without making promises you can't keep. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T3#GNS315_U5_T3_h8)

question: What is the main goal when medical help arrives immediately after a disaster?

options.A: To minimize death and illness
options.B: To train local volunteers
options.C: To rebuild damaged hospitals
options.D: To document insurance claims

explanation: You've got this! When disaster strikes, the immediate focus is always on saving lives and stopping severe illness through quick medical action. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why do nurses have to change how they normally work when responding to a field disaster?

options.A: Basic utilities and sterile spaces are usually missing
options.B: Patients refuse standard medications in the field
options.C: Disaster protocols completely forbid using medications
options.D: Physicians are rarely present during emergencies

explanation: Great thinking! Out in the field, you won't find normal hospital comforts like constant running water or steady electricity, so nurses have to adapt cleverly and safely. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h1)

question: In a mass casualty incident, what does a RED triage tag mean?

options.A: Minor injuries that can wait until the end of the shift
options.B: Immediate life-threatening injuries with a high chance of survival
options.C: Injuries so severe that survival is unlikely
options.D: Deceased patients who need no further attention

explanation: Spot on! Red means urgent. It tells us the patient has a life-threatening problem that we can fix right now to save their life. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h2)

question: A patient in a disaster zone has a severe head injury, is unresponsive, breathing irregularly, and has no pulse. Which triage category fits best?

options.A: Red
options.B: Black
options.C: Yellow
options.D: Green

explanation: You're doing great. A black tag (or expectant) is used for catastrophic injuries where survival is sadly very unlikely, helping us save resources for those we can help. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h2)

question: What is the absolute first thing a nurse checks during an initial trauma assessment?

options.A: Pain assessment
options.B: Airway management
options.C: Wound dressing
options.D: Checking blood pressure

explanation: Think ABCs! Keeping the airway open is always step one because a blocked airway causes a patient to deteriorate the fastest. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h3)

question: Why is stopping heavy bleeding such a high priority in disaster trauma care?

options.A: Clean bandages are always in short supply
options.B: Blood spills make the clinical environment too slippery
options.C: Patients feel less pain if bleeding stops right away
options.D: Unchecked hemorrhage quickly leads to fatal hemorrhagic shock

explanation: Spot on! Uncontrolled bleeding causes blood pressure to crash rapidly, which can quickly become fatal if we don't jump in fast. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h3)

question: Where is the best spot to set up a temporary disaster field hospital?

options.A: Directly inside an unstable damaged building
options.B: In the deepest part of the flooded zone
options.C: As far away from the disaster victims as possible
options.D: On stable, accessible ground away from immediate hazards

explanation: Makes total sense! We want a safe, solid spot that ambulances and walking patients can easily reach without getting caught in secondary dangers. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h4)

question: Why is proper waste disposal so important right from the start in a field hospital?

options.A: To make the area look neat for visiting leaders
options.B: To comply with local parking regulations
options.C: To prevent secondary disease outbreaks in the camp
options.D: To ensure the medical tents do not blow away

explanation: You got it! Leftover medical and human waste quickly breeds harmful germs, turning the camp into a new sick zone if we aren't careful. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h4)

question: What is a major danger when a trapped victim is finally freed from a prolonged crush injury?

options.A: Crush syndrome and acute kidney failure
options.B: Immediate high blood pressure spikes
options.C: Sudden permanent blindness
options.D: Instantaneous bone hardening

explanation: Brilliant! When crushed muscles are released, they dump toxins like potassium and myoglobin into the blood, which can overwhelm and shut down the kidneys. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why are IV fluids given to a patient with a severe crush injury before they are freed?

options.A: To prevent external skin infections
options.B: To numb the pain of broken bones
options.C: To make the patient sleep through the rescue
options.D: To flush out toxins and protect the kidneys

explanation: That's right! Pumping in fluids helps dilute and flush those nasty muscle toxins through the kidneys safely before they can cause severe damage. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h5)

question: Which type of illness spreads the fastest in crowded, poorly sanitized relief camps?

options.A: Degenerative joint diseases
options.B: Chronic autoimmune conditions
options.C: Waterborne infectious diseases
options.D: Hereditary metabolic disorders

explanation: Spot on! When clean water and toilets break down, infections like cholera and dysentery spread through the camp like wildfire. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h6)

question: What is your first nursing action if a patient in a relief camp presents with severe watery diarrhea?

options.A: Prescribe heavy exercise to boost immunity
options.B: Send the patient home immediately
options.C: Restrict all fluid intake to rest the bowel
options.D: Isolate the patient and initiate rehydration therapy

explanation: You're on the right track! Isolating stops it from spreading to others, while rehydration replaces all those lost body fluids immediately. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h6)

question: What is the main focus of Psychological First Aid (PFA) in a disaster?

options.A: Providing humane practical support and reducing distress
options.B: Conducting formal psychoanalysis sessions
options.C: Prescribing strong antidepressant medications
options.D: Diagnosing deep psychiatric disorders

explanation: Well done! PFA isn't about heavy therapy or psychoanalysis; it's about being human, offering practical comfort, and helping people feel safe. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why must disaster nurses actively watch out for compassion fatigue and practice self-care?

options.A: Patients will lose respect for nurses who show emotion
options.B: Nurses are immune to stress if they work fast enough
options.C: Hospital managers require daily wellness logs from every nurse
options.D: Prolonged exposure to trauma can lead to severe emotional burnout

explanation: So true! Seeing constant suffering wears down even the strongest nurses. Taking care of your own mental health keeps you and your patients safe. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h7)

question: What is a major headache when trying to move medical supplies into a disaster zone?

options.A: Instantaneous electronic inventory updates everywhere
options.B: Damaged transport routes and broken infrastructure
options.C: Too many delivery trucks crowding the roads
options.D: Excessive amounts of clean storage space

explanation: You got it! When bridges collapse and roads are blocked with debris, getting medical boxes delivered becomes an extreme logistical puzzle. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h8)

question: Why do nurses need to track daily medication use closely in a field clinic?

options.A: To calculate daily hospital profits for insurance
options.B: To keep pharmacy staff busy with paperwork
options.C: To predict shortages and reorder supplies before running out
options.D: To prove to patients that drugs are expensive

explanation: Smart nursing! Keeping an eye on daily counts helps you spot when you're running low so you can reorder life-saving items ahead of time. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h8)

question: What is a crucial nursing duty BEFORE transferring a stabilized disaster victim to another hospital?

options.A: Remove all wound dressings for final inspection
options.B: Discontinue all intravenous fluids to save equipment
options.C: Wait for family members to sign financial clearance
options.D: Ensure secure lines, stable vitals, and handover notes

explanation: Spot on! Before they roll out, make sure their IV lines are secure, vitals are stable, and the receiving team has clear notes to continue good care. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h9)

question: Why is clear documentation so important during patient transfers in a disaster?

options.A: It prevents the ambulance driver from getting lost
options.B: It informs the receiving team of treatments already given
options.C: It guarantees the patient will recover faster
options.D: It serves as a legal ticket for free transport

explanation: Great job! Good handover notes stop medication errors and make sure the next team knows exactly what you've already done for the patient. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h9)

question: Which ethical rule guides how resources are shared when supplies are very scarce during a disaster?

options.A: Giving the newest supplies only to wealthy donors
options.B: Treating every person strictly on a first-come, first-served basis
options.C: Justice and doing the greatest good for the greatest number
options.D: Refusing care until formal legal contracts are signed

explanation: You've got it! In mass disasters, we shift from treating just one person to figuring out how to do the greatest good for the whole community fairly. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h10)

question: What makes ethical choices so emotionally heavy for nurses during a major disaster?

options.A: Having to ration scarce life-saving resources among many needy patients
options.B: Having too many modern medical machines to choose from
options.C: Working in fully air-conditioned and quiet field offices
options.D: Patients having unlimited time to discuss treatment options

explanation: So true. Deciding who gets scarce life-saving care when there isn't enough to go around is one of the hardest emotional burdens a nurse can carry. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T4#GNS315_U5_T4_h10)

question: Right after a disaster strikes, what is the main thing nurses and responders focus on first?

options.A: Replacing damaged hospital buildings permanently
options.B: Protecting human life and stabilizing the injured
options.C: Conducting long-term epidemiological research
options.D: Providing financial loans to displaced families

explanation: When an emergency hits, your immediate priority as a nurse is always saving lives and keeping people stable before worrying about anything else. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h1)

question: How does your job as a nurse change when you step out of a normal hospital and into a disaster zone?

options.A: The nurse only focuses on administrative paperwork
options.B: The nurse must rely more on quick improvisations and resource-scarce settings
options.C: The nurse works exclusively with advanced robotic surgical tools
options.D: The nurse stops providing direct patient care entirely

explanation: Disasters mess up normal hospital supplies, so you'll often have to think on your feet and make the best of what's available around you. It's tough, but Nigerian nurses do it brilliantly! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h1)

question: During triage at a disaster scene, which color tag goes to patients who can walk and only have minor cuts or scrapes?

options.A: Red
options.B: Black
options.C: Yellow
options.D: Green

explanation: Think of 'Green' like a green light—these are the walking wounded who are stable and don't need emergency rushing to the theatre. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h2)

question: A patient tagged as yellow suddenly starts gasping for air and showing signs of shock. What should you do?

options.A: Ask the patient to walk over to the green area
options.B: Leave the patient in the yellow category because triage tags never change
options.C: Re-tag the patient as red and provide immediate life-saving care
options.D: Move the patient to the black category immediately

explanation: Triage isn't a one-time thing; patient conditions change fast! If someone gets worse, you upgrade their tag right away to get them urgent help. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h2)

question: When setting up a temporary camp for people displaced by a disaster, which type of location should you strictly avoid?

options.A: Flat land with easy access to roads
options.B: Areas far away from stagnant water bodies
options.C: Locations with proper ventilation and spacing
options.D: Flood-prone zones and landslide-risk areas

explanation: Putting a camp in a swampy or flood-prone area just invites another disaster. Always look for high, safe ground! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why is it so important to leave enough space between tents when setting up a temporary disaster camp?

options.A: It helps prevent the rapid spread of airborne and contact illnesses
options.B: It ensures everyone gets the exact same size tent
options.C: It makes the camp look more organized for visitors
options.D: It allows heavy machinery to drive through the tents at night

explanation: When people are packed too tightly together, illnesses like coughs and infections spread like wildfire. Space keeps everyone safer! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h3)

question: What major health threat usually pops up first when clean water supplies and sewage systems break down during a disaster?

options.A: Waterborne disease outbreaks like cholera
options.B: Widespread Vitamin D deficiency
options.C: Chronic bone fractures
options.D: Sudden increases in genetic disorders

explanation: When sewage mixes with drinking water, tummy troubles and deadly infections like cholera follow fast. Safe water is lifesaving! [learn more](GNS315_U5_T5#GNS315_U5_T5_h4)

question: Why do emergency planners insist that temporary latrines must be built downhill and far away from community water sources?

question: Why are Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF) so popular for feeding hungry children early in a disaster?

options.B: They taste sweet and only appeal to adults

question: Why must used needles and medical waste be disposed of with extreme care in a disaster camp?

question: What is the primary nature of psychological trauma experienced during a disaster?

options.D: A sign of personal weakness or poor upbringing

question: Which hormones are primarily released by the body during an acute stress response?

options.C: Insulin and glucagon

options.D: Sedate, Calm, Rest
